# Optimisation and cost

Token prices are assumptions for modelling (2026-11-09 (assumed list-price-style figures for modelling, not quotes; verify before use)): small tier $0.0003 and large tier $0.0030 per 1K tokens, blended input and output. Latency is the sum of declared per-tool and per-model latencies (simulated). All numbers are averages per request over each domain's synthetic suite.

## Cost drivers

| Driver | Where it comes from | Control in this design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model tokens | parse, reply drafting, plan drafting, policy answers | rule code, templates, small context, answer cache |
| Model tier | every model call | router: small tier for easy work, cascade on schema failure |
| Tool calls | reads and writes | memoised reads, batched reads, idempotent replays |
| Retries and repairs | timeouts, lost replies, malformed output | capped retries, one repair, then a person |
| Latency | tools + model calls in sequence | fewer calls, small tier, batched reads |
| Runaway work | loops, large prompts | per-request caps: 14 tool calls, 2600 tokens, 9000 ms (simulated) |

Before = every cost optimisation off (full context to the model, model-written plans and replies, always the large tier, no answer cache, one read per call). After = all on. Safety layers are on in both.

Notes:

- `context_trim` alone saves money only because, in the unoptimised build, a model reads the context to draft plans and replies. Once rule code and templates replace those calls, it mainly protects privacy and the token cap.
- `routing` can raise token counts slightly (a cascade re-asks the large tier when the small tier's answer fails validation) while cutting cost, because most requests are easy.
- `batch_reads` saves tool calls and latency, not tokens.
- The simulated model is assumed to be equally correct in both builds, which flatters the unoptimised build; in practice fewer model calls also means fewer chances to be wrong.
